title: Spritz Cookies EVERYONE's Grandma Made (Why Yours Won't STICK)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, spritz cookies are the little butter cookies pressed into Christmas trees, wreaths, and stars that were on every cookie tray in America. Crisp at the edges, tender in the middle, and they melt on your tongue. But most people who try them give up after ten minutes, because the dough won't come out of the press, or it won't stick to the pan. And it's always the same five mistakes.
scenes.query: tray of spritz cookies shaped like trees and wreaths
scenes.caption: IT WON'T STICK

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you the spritz cookies my mother made every December on Elm Street, step by step, with the cookie press my father gave her in nineteen fifty-one. And stay with me, because the last secret is where she put her cookie sheets before every batch, and it's the reason hers never failed. You probably have the same thing outside your back door right now.
scenes.query: vintage aluminum cookie press 1950s
scenes.caption: OUTSIDE YOUR BACK DOOR

scenes.text: Spritz cookies came from Germany and Scandinavia, honey. The word comes from the German spritzen, which means to squirt, because you squirt the dough through a press. The German and Swedish families who settled in Ohio and Wisconsin and Minnesota brought them, and by the nineteen fifties, a cookie press was one of the most popular Christmas presents in the country. Every bride got one.
scenes.query: old German Christmas bakery cookies
scenes.caption: TO SQUIRT

scenes.text: My father bought my mother hers at Halle's department store in Cleveland, in nineteen fifty-one. An aluminum tube with a crank on the top and a little box of metal discs, a tree, a wreath, a star, a camel, a flower, a dog. It cost three dollars and forty cents, which was a lot. She was so excited she made cookies the same night, and every single one came out a blob. In a minute I'll tell you why.
scenes.query: cookie press with metal shape discs in box
scenes.caption: EVERY ONE A BLOB

scenes.text: She cried, honey. She really did. And my father, who never baked a thing in his life, sat down with the little instruction booklet and read it out loud, every word, while she tried again. And by the end of the night, they had two dozen perfect little trees, and flour all over both of them. She used that press every Christmas for thirty-eight years. I use it now. It still works.
scenes.query: couple in 1950s kitchen covered in flour laughing
scenes.caption: 38 CHRISTMASES

scenes.text: Those cookie presses were made right here in the Midwest, honey, and every company had its own little set of shapes. Some had a Christmas camel, some had a butterfly, and one had a little Scottie dog that every child fought over. Collectors pay good money for the old boxed sets now. Ours still has the original instruction booklet, with my father's pencil notes in the margin.
scenes.query: vintage cookie press box and booklet
scenes.caption: THE SCOTTIE DOG

scenes.text: Here's what you need for about six dozen cookies. One cup of real butter, two sticks, softened. Two thirds of a cup of sugar. One egg. One teaspoon of vanilla extract. A half teaspoon of almond extract, which is the old-fashioned flavor everybody remembers. Two and a quarter cups of all-purpose flour. And a half teaspoon of salt. That's all. No baking powder, honey. Spritz cookies don't rise. That's how they hold their shape.
scenes.query: butter sugar flour egg and extracts on counter
scenes.caption: NO BAKING POWDER

scenes.text: For decorating, you need colored sugar, red and green, and little cinnamon candies, and nonpareils. And if you want green trees and pink wreaths, a few drops of food coloring in the dough. And of course, a cookie press. You can find the old metal ones at any thrift store for a few dollars, and they work better than most of the new plastic ones. Or ask your grandmother. She's got one in a drawer somewhere.
scenes.query: colored sugar sprinkles in small bowls
scenes.caption: ASK YOUR GRANDMOTHER

scenes.text: Mistake number one is butter that's too soft or too hard. If the butter's melted, the cookies spread into blobs. If it's cold, the dough is too stiff to come out of the press. Leave it on the counter about an hour, until you can press a dent in it with your finger, but it still holds its shape. Beat the butter and sugar together for three minutes, until it's pale and fluffy.
scenes.query: finger pressing dent in softened butter
scenes.caption: A DENT, NOT A PUDDLE

scenes.text: If Grandma's recipe is helping you, tap the like button for me, sweetheart. It helps more people find these videos. Mistake number two is too much flour. Measure it the right way. Spoon the flour into your measuring cup and level it off with a knife. Don't scoop the cup into the bag, because that packs it in, and you end up with a dry dough that cracks in the press. Then beat in the egg and extracts, and stir in the flour and salt, just until it's smooth.
scenes.query: spooning flour into measuring cup and leveling
scenes.caption: SPOON AND LEVEL

scenes.text: And here's something most recipes get wrong, honey. Don't chill spritz dough. Every other cookie dough, you chill. Not this one. Cold spritz dough won't go through the press. You want it soft and pliable, about like play clay. Pack it into the press right away, while it's still at room temperature. In a minute I'll tell you the one thing that should be cold.
scenes.query: soft cookie dough packed into press tube
scenes.caption: DON'T CHILL THE DOUGH

scenes.text: Mistake number three is greasing the pan, or using parchment paper or a silicone mat. That's why most people's cookies won't stick. The way a cookie press works is, the dough has to grab onto the pan, so when you lift the press, the cookie stays behind. On a greased pan or parchment, it just lifts right back up with the press. Use a plain, ungreased, uncoated metal cookie sheet. Nothing on it at all.
scenes.query: plain bare metal cookie sheet
scenes.caption: NOTHING ON THE PAN

scenes.text: Hold the press straight up and down, with the bottom resting flat on the pan. Give the crank or the trigger one full click. Then lift the press straight up. Don't tilt it, don't drag it. One click, lift, move over an inch, one click, lift. Your first two or three will be ugly, honey. Everybody's are. Scrape them off and put the dough back in the press. After a few, you'll find your rhythm.
scenes.query: pressing cookies in rows on baking sheet
scenes.caption: ONE CLICK, LIFT

scenes.text: If the dough won't come out at all, honey, it's too stiff. Take the dough out, work in a teaspoon of milk with your hands, and try again. If the cookies come out but spread and lose their lines, the dough is too soft or the kitchen is too warm. Work in a tablespoon of flour. Don't give up after the first try. Even my mother cried the first night. I'll tell you how the cookie sheet fixes most of this in a minute.
scenes.query: hands kneading milk into cookie dough
scenes.caption: DON'T GIVE UP

scenes.text: So far, butter with a dent, spoon and level, don't chill the dough, and a bare metal pan. Mistake number four is putting the next batch on a warm pan. The butter in the dough melts the second it touches a warm sheet, and the cookie won't hold its shape or stick. Always let your pans cool all the way between batches. Use two or three pans and rotate them. Stay with me, because this is connected to the secret.
scenes.query: hot cookie sheet cooling on counter
scenes.caption: NEVER A WARM PAN

scenes.text: Sprinkle the colored sugar on right away, before they bake, so it sticks. Then bake at three hundred seventy-five degrees for six to eight minutes. Mistake number five is overbaking. Spritz cookies should be pale on top, with just the faintest golden edge on the bottom. If they're brown, they taste like cardboard. Let them sit on the pan for one minute, then move them to a rack with a thin spatula.
scenes.query: pale spritz cookies with colored sugar on rack
scenes.caption: PALE ON TOP

scenes.text: Here's my mother's secret, sweetheart. Before every single batch, she set her empty cookie sheets out on the back porch, in the snow, for five minutes. Ohio in December, honey. The porch was a refrigerator. And she pressed the cookies onto those ice-cold metal sheets. The dough grabs onto cold metal like it's glued there. Every cookie sticks. Every edge stays sharp. Not one blob.
scenes.query: cookie sheets cooling in snow on back porch
scenes.caption: THE PORCH WAS A REFRIGERATOR

scenes.text: If you don't have snow, put your bare sheet in the freezer for ten minutes, or in the refrigerator for twenty. Just the sheet, honey, never the dough. Cold pan, soft dough. That's the whole trick. My father figured it out from the instruction booklet that first night. It said, use cool baking sheets. And my mother said, Walter, if cool is good, cold is better. And she was right.
scenes.query: bare cookie sheet going into freezer
scenes.caption: COLD PAN, SOFT DOUGH

scenes.text: For green trees, mix a few drops of green coloring into half the dough. Put a single cinnamon candy on top of each one, like a star. For wreaths, use plain dough, dip the tops in green sugar, and put three tiny red candies at the bottom for berries. You can also dip half of each cooled cookie in melted chocolate and lay it on wax paper to set. Children love doing that part.
scenes.query: green tree spritz cookies with red candy stars
scenes.caption: TREES AND WREATHS

scenes.text: They keep for two weeks in a tin, honey, with wax paper between the layers, and they freeze beautifully for two months. My mother made twelve dozen every year. She packed them in coffee cans with Christmas paper glued around the outside, and gave them to the mailman, the milkman, the minister, and every widow on our street. Danny and I delivered them on our sleds.
scenes.query: coffee cans wrapped in Christmas paper full of cookies
scenes.caption: DELIVERED ON SLEDS

scenes.text: Make them this week, sweetheart, and don't forget to chill those pans. Tell me in the comments, did your grandmother have a cookie press? Which shape was your favorite? There are more of my Christmas recipes in the playlist right there on your screen. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.query: Christmas cookie tray with spritz cookies
scenes.caption: WHICH SHAPE?
